newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa eyes budget to flesh out Mandela promises.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa eyes budget to flesh out Mandela promises.

text.p: South African markets gave President Nelson Mandela a warm reception on Friday as he mapped out economic reforms for the year ahead, including the imminent privatisation of key state assets.

The rand rallied to a 6-1/2 month high, but analysts said Finance Minister Trevor Manuel would have to reinforce Mandela's promises with hard numbers and with concrete proposals on dismantling exchange controls to retain the markets' new-found confidence.
"Expectations have now been raised and this must be followed by actions in the budget (on March 12)," said Dave Mohr, chief economist at life assurance giant Old Mutual in Cape Town.

"The government has got to illustrate that it is serious in reducing the budget deficit, reducing government consumption spending and further relaxing exchange controls. We have confirmed that we are on the right road, that we are not going to make a U-turn, but we need to convince markets with action."

Despite the lack of any concrete announcement on easing exchange controls, which some had hoped for, analysts said a window of opportunity remained for the government to produce firm plans around the time of the March 12 budget.

These could focus on new steps to allow institutions to invest more money offshore, moves to permit foreign currency bank accounts within South Africa and the withdrawal of the central bank from the forward foreign exchange market.

Action to free some 10 billion rand ($2.25 billion) of blocked rand accounts -- money which emigrants were forced to leave in South Africa -- is expected only towards the end of a gradual relaxation process.
Exactly a year ago, Mandela delivered a similarly upbeat assessment of South Africa's economic prospects to the opening of the 1996 session of parliament.
A week later the rand tumbled amid rumours over his health and an influential report from investment house UBS saying the currency was overvalued.
One year on, the tide has finally turned and the bulls have returned in force to South Africa's markets.

Foreigners have poured more than three billion rand into South African bonds this year and some economists are nervous about volatile portfolio inflows, which can be pulled out as fast as they went in.
But the fundamental political and economic picture is different in some key respects:
- much of the uncertainty about the Mandela succession has been resolved with Deputy President Thabo Mbeki now widely accepted as heir apparent when Mandela steps down in 1999;
- the government appears well on track to cut its budget deficit to 5.1 percent of GDP this year and 4.0 percent next;
- the trade balance has improved sharply, pointing to a big cut in the current account deficit and a rise in reserves;
- the government has committed itself to a coherent market-oriented economic growth plan in its Growth, Redistribution and Employment strategy;
- and the rand, which most analysts agreed was over-valued in early 1996, is now generally perceived as under-valued in terms of purchasing power parity.
